M., Uszkoreit, J., Le, Q., and Petrov, S. (2019). Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, vol. 7, pp. 453–466. https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00276
creator: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, Slav Petrov (Google Research)
description: Natural Questions (NQ) is a large-scale question answering dataset where questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. Annotators are presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results and annotate a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or mark null if no answer is present. The public release consists of 307,373 training examples with single annotations, 7,830 development examples with 5-way annotations, and 7,842 test examples with 5-way annotations.
name: Natural Questions
rai:annotationsPerItem: Training examples have single annotations (1-way); development and test examples have 5-way annotations; a subset of 302 examples has 25-way annotations for quality analysis.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was evaluated via two methods: (1) Post hoc expert evaluation — four experts (the first four authors) independently annotated 139 sampled examples for correctness (Correct, Correct-but-debatable, Wrong), then reached consensus judgments. Long answer precision was 90% and short answer precision was 84%. (2) 25-way annotations on 302 examples to study variability — the proportion of non-null annotations (μ) was found to be highly correlated with annotation precision. The most popular long answer accounts for 83% of annotations; the most popular short answer accounts for 64%. Single annotator F1 was 73.4% for long answers and 57.5% for short answers, while the super-annotator upper bound was 87.2% F1 for long answers and 75.7% for short answers.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation is performed using a custom annotation interface by a pool of around 50 annotators, with an average annotation time of 80 seconds. The annotation task is divided into three conceptual stages completed by a single annotator in succession: (1) Question Identification — annotator determines whether the question is good (fact-seeking, answerable with an entity or explanation) or bad (ambiguous, incomprehensible, opinion-seeking, etc.); (2) Long Answer Identification — for good questions, annotator selects the earliest HTML bounding box (paragraph, table, list item, or whole list) containing enough information to infer the answer, or marks 'no answer'; (3) Short Answer Identification — for examples with long answers, annotator selects the entity or set of entities within the long answer, or flags yes/no, or flags no short answer possible. Comprehensive guidelines were developed and annotation quality was constantly monitored.
rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges that focusing on Wikipedia as the evidence source may introduce biases, as Wikipedia is a specific source of factual information with its own stylistic and content biases. The paper notes that future data collection efforts may introduce shorter queries, 'how to' questions, or domains other than Wikipedia. Questions are also limited to those of 8 words or more, focusing on longer, more complex queries.
rai:dataCollection: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries of 8 words or more issued to the Google search engine by multiple users in a short period of time. Simple heuristics are used to filter questions from the query stream (e.g., questions starting with 'who', 'when', 'where', or containing multiple entities). Questions are run through the Google search engine and kept only where there is a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results. The resulting (question, Wikipedia page) pairs are then presented to human annotators who identify long and short answers.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine (queries of 8 words or more issued by multiple users in a short period of time), paired with Wikipedia pages returned in the top 5 search results for each query.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses only on Wikipedia as the evidence source, which may not generalize to other domains. Questions are limited to those of 8 words or more, excluding shorter queries and 'how to' questions. There is genuine ambiguity in whether or not an answer is acceptable for naturally occurring questions, leading to annotator variability. Boolean (yes/no) answers are not addressed in the baseline experiments and are left to future work. The test set is sequestered and not publicly released.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were filtered from the Google search query stream using heuristics to retain fact-seeking questions of 8 words or more: filters include questions starting with 'who', 'when', 'where' followed by specific grammatical patterns, questions containing multiple entities with adjectives/adverbs/verbs/determiners, and questions ending with categorical noun phrases. Part-of-speech tags and entities were identified using Google's Cloud NLP API. Questions were further filtered to retain only those with a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is designed to have genuine utility to users as it is based on real information-seeking queries. The authors argue that a solution to Natural Questions will have genuine utility as a benchmark for NLU, and that progress on QA has been hindered by a lack of appropriate training and test data. The dataset is intended to drive significant advances in natural language understanding.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as: (1) a large-scale end-to-end training dataset for the question answering problem; (2) a benchmark dataset to drive research in natural language understanding (NLU); (3) a resource for studying human performance in providing QA annotations for naturally occurring questions. It is designed to evaluate open-domain question answering systems that must identify both a long answer (paragraph-level) and a short answer (entity-level) from Wikipedia pages.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google's Cloud NLP API (https://cloud.google.com/natural-language) was used to identify part-of-speech tags and named entities during question filtering. Hearst patterns were used to pre-define categorical noun phrases for heuristic filters.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Questions are real queries from Google search but are anonymized and aggregated to protect user privacy.

null_reasons.rai:annotatorDemographics: The paper only mentions a pool of around 50 annotators with no demographic information provided.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe or date range for data collection is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: No discussion of missing data handling in the collection process; queries without Wikipedia pages in top 5 results are simply discarded rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol described; missing/null answers are retained as NULL labels rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection data manipulation, augmentation, or resampling described for the dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan described in the paper.
